# Weekly Multi-Asset Market Briefing – Buy-Side Strategy Narrative

The past week in markets was defined by a sharp factor rotation beneath relatively contained index-level moves, with investors decisively favoring semiconductors and select energy cyclicals while taking profits across higher-multiple software, cybersecurity, and marketing technology. Software infrastructure, application software, and security all traded heavy, with many high-quality franchises experiencing mid–single-digit to low–double-digit drawdowns, even in the absence of company-specific catalysts. At the same time, a powerful bid in memory, AI-adjacent semis, and offshore energy generated outsized gains in a subset of cyclicals, led by Micron, Sable Offshore Corp., and a cluster of smaller semiconductor names. Against a macro backdrop still dominated by the path of policy rates and the durability of nominal growth, this divergence in performance underscores a market that is becoming more discriminating on valuation, more selective within the “AI trade,” and more sensitive to positioning and liquidity rather than to fundamentals alone.

## Market Overview

The dominant feature of the week was not a dramatic move in headline equity indices but rather a meaningful change in leadership beneath the surface. While broad benchmarks appeared comparatively orderly, sector and factor dispersion reached levels that felt more like a mini-rotation than a quiet summer week. In particular, there was a pronounced de-rating across a wide swath of software and growth-exposed financial technology, where many names saw share price declines between roughly six and eleven percent over the week, while cyclical pockets of the market, especially semiconductors and energy, advanced strongly. This pattern is consistent with a market that is rebalancing from crowded beneficiaries of lower-rate expectations toward companies with more tangible operating leverage to nominal growth and secular demand.

Software infrastructure and application software exhibited some of the most notable weakness. Within software infrastructure, Palantir, JFrog, Amplitude, MongoDB, Samsara, Fair Isaac, Procore, and Elastic all posted weekly declines spanning mid–single-digit to low–double-digit percentages, with Palantir down about 11.1 percent, JFrog down 11.0 percent, and Amplitude down 8.4 percent. Application software traded similarly poorly, with Guidewire, DocuSign, Intuit, BlackLine, Workday, RingCentral, Freshworks, and Asana all under pressure; Guidewire declined 8.7 percent, DocuSign 7.3 percent, Intuit 7.0 percent, and Workday 6.8 percent over the week. The breadth and synchrony of these moves, in the absence of a dense earnings calendar, point more to factor and flows dynamics than to any fundamental deterioration across the group.

Cybersecurity, previously a perceived safe-haven within high-growth technology due to resilient demand and mission-critical products, also succumbed to selling pressure. Rapid7, CrowdStrike, Tenable, Okta, and Qualys all saw declines of roughly five to seven percent on the week, while Palo Alto Networks, Varonis, and Check Point were somewhat more resilient but still finished lower in the mid–single-digit range. This group had been trading at a premium to the broader software complex, supported by secular tailwinds such as cloud adoption, remote work, and increasing threat complexity. The synchronized drawdown across the basket suggests that investors are increasingly willing to rotate out of even high-quality, secular growth names when valuations feel stretched and alternatives with more cyclical torque—such as semiconductors and select energy—become more attractive.

In sharp contrast, semiconductors put in a notably strong performance and reaffirmed their role as the market’s preferred expression of the AI and high-performance computing theme. Within the watchlist, Micron rallied 10.8 percent for the week and is now up 34.7 percent over the past month, while Sandisk advanced 10.1 percent on the week and 41.6 percent over the past month. Intel gained 8.8 percent for the week despite being down 10.0 percent over the past month, and Astera Labs rose 7.3 percent, extending its one-month gain to 17.7 percent. Taiwan Semiconductor added 5.5 percent on the week and 8.2 percent over the month, while POET Technologies climbed 5.1 percent and is now up 19.1 percent over the last month. These moves underscore the persistent preference for AI-levered hardware, particularly where near-term earnings revisions remain positive and capacity tightness continues to support pricing.

Energy and industrial cyclicals also saw renewed interest, led by Sable Offshore Corp., which surged 37.5 percent for the week and an impressive 124.7 percent over the past month. Within exploration and production, Occidental advanced 6.3 percent and Devon Energy 6.2 percent week-on-week, with California Resources up 5.3 percent as well. On the industrial side, names such as Comfort Systems (FIX) and Baker Hughes advanced in the low–to mid–single-digit range, highlighting the incremental appetite for real asset exposure and cash-generative cyclicals. The interplay between these “hard asset” trades and the ongoing bid for semiconductors suggests that investors are constructing barbell portfolios: pairing AI-centric growth with energy and industrials that offer inflation resilience and positive free cash flow.

AdTech, digital media, and marketing technology, meanwhile, represented another pocket of notable weakness. AppLovin fell 13.4 percent week-on-week and is down 6.6 percent over the last month, while Klaviyo declined 10.0 percent on the week and is roughly flat over the month. LiveRamp and Braze fell 8.3 percent and 8.1 percent, respectively, with LiveRamp also down 6.1 percent over the month and Braze still up 10.8 percent over that horizon. Sprinklr slid 5.2 percent for the week, while other marketing and data-driven advertising plays like Zeta Global and The Trade Desk fell more mildly. Taken together, these moves highlight a market that is re-pricing the more speculative parts of the consumption and advertising ecosystem, especially where valuations leaned on elevated growth expectations and where competitive dynamics remain intense.

Consumer and e-commerce exposures on the watchlist also faced a difficult tape. Shopify declined 8.0 percent on the week and 1.8 percent over the month, with GoDaddy down 6.7 percent and 8.9 percent over those horizons. Global-e Online and Wix both traded off in the mid–single-digit range, and even some higher-quality, more defensive consumer names such as General Mills posted moderate losses. There were, however, pockets of relative strength within consumer, including Nike, which added 3.9 percent on the week, and select emerging-market consumer technology names such as SEA, which advanced 2.9 percent. This mixed picture in consumer underscores the extent to which the market is differentiating between discretionary and staple demand, pricing power, and exposure to macro uncertainty.

Finally, fintech and payments saw broad-based pressure, with Bill Holdings down 8.5 percent on the week and 2.3 percent over the month, Global Payments down 6.0 percent and 5.5 percent, and others such as Block (if considered by proxy via peer group), Marqeta, and card issuers under moderate pressure. Within the watchlist, other fintech-related names such as LPL Financial, Affirm, and Synchrony Financial also saw smaller losses. These moves appear consistent with a cautious stance toward consumer credit and small-business activity, along with the general de-rating seen in higher-beta growth names.

## Sector Leadership & Rotation

The most salient theme in sector leadership this week was the divergence between semiconductors and software. Semiconductors, as captured by Micron, Sandisk, Intel, Astera Labs, Taiwan Semiconductor, POET, and Teradyne, delivered strong gains that significantly outpaced the broader technology complex. Micron’s 10.8 percent weekly advance and 34.7 percent monthly gain, alongside Sandisk’s 10.1 percent weekly and 41.6 percent monthly performance, underscore the intensity of the bid for memory and storage exposures that are critical to AI and cloud datacenter build-outs. Even Intel, despite being down 10.0 percent over the month, rebounded 8.8 percent this week, suggesting that investors are opportunistically adding to legacy CPU and foundry-transition stories when they reset.

The breadth of the semiconductor rally is noteworthy. Astera Labs, a higher-growth enabler for AI interconnect and systems, rose 7.3 percent on the week and 17.7 percent over the month, while POET, a smaller-cap player with exposure to photonics and advanced chip architectures, gained 5.1 percent on the week and 19.1 percent over the past month. Taiwan Semiconductor’s 5.5 percent weekly and 8.2 percent monthly gains reflect continued conviction that leading-edge foundry capacity is an essential bottleneck in the AI value chain. Teradyne, another watchlist name focused on test equipment, delivered a 4.3 percent weekly rise, highlighting that downstream supplier ecosystems are also participating in the move. This pattern reinforces the notion that the AI trade is broadening beyond a handful of mega-cap GPU providers into the wider hardware value chain.

In energy and industrials, leadership was anchored by Sable Offshore Corp., where the stock’s 37.5 percent weekly and 124.7 percent monthly gains stand out even within a strong energy tape. While the absence of a near-term earnings catalyst points toward positioning, contract wins, or asset revaluation as likely drivers, the magnitude and persistence of the move indicate that investors are increasingly willing to underwrite higher risk in offshore and exploration-related plays. Occidental’s 6.3 percent and Devon’s 6.2 percent weekly gains, alongside California Resources’ 5.3 percent, reinforce that the market remains receptive to E&P stories offering leverage to commodity prices, capital return, and operational efficiency. Within industrial services, Comfort Systems’ 4.1 percent weekly gain and Baker Hughes’ 4.2 percent advance further emphasize the appetite for companies tied to infrastructure, energy services, and the industrial capex cycle.

By contrast, software—particularly the higher-multiple corners of the space—experienced a broad-based derating. The software infrastructure basket, comprising Palantir, JFrog, Amplitude, MongoDB, Samsara, Fair Isaac, Procore, and Elastic, was under pressure across the board. Palantir’s 11.1 percent weekly decline and JFrog’s 11.0 percent loss sit at the extreme, but the entire group faced meaningful selling, with Amplitude down 8.4 percent and MongoDB down 8.3 percent. Samsara’s 7.0 percent weekly decline, Fair Isaac’s 6.3 percent, Procore’s 6.0 percent, and Elastic’s 5.7 percent round out the picture. It is notable that this weakness came despite the absence of a dense upcoming earnings calendar and limited company-specific news, implying that valuation and positioning were more significant drivers than revised expectations of demand.

Application software showed an almost identical pattern of weakness. Guidewire declined 8.7 percent, DocuSign 7.3 percent, Intuit 7.0 percent, BlackLine 6.9 percent, Workday 6.8 percent, RingCentral 6.7 percent, Freshworks 6.5 percent, and Asana 6.1 percent. With many of these companies operating in relatively stable end markets such as financial services software, tax and accounting tools, back-office automation, and HR and collaboration, their simultaneous drawdown points toward a common narrative: investors increasingly demand either clear AI monetization pathways or tangible operating leverage to justify premium multiples. Names lacking a near-term AI revenue kicker, or those where AI is perceived as a longer-dated optionality rather than an immediate driver, appear more vulnerable to de-rating when macro uncertainty or rate volatility rises.

Cybersecurity experienced similar selling pressure, albeit from an already premium valuation base. Rapid7’s 7.3 percent weekly decline was among the worst in the group, followed by Tenable at 5.7 percent, CrowdStrike at 5.7 percent, Okta at 5.6 percent, and Qualys at 5.3 percent, with Palo Alto Networks, Varonis, and Check Point also lower by mid–single-digit percentages. These companies generally continue to benefit from durable demand for cloud security, identity management, endpoint protection, and vulnerability management, but the narrative has shifted from purely top-line growth to a more balanced focus on profitability and free cash flow. When investors rotate toward semiconductors and energy, security becomes a source of funds, particularly for those who had previously built large overweight positions in this perceived secular compounder cohort.

AdTech and marketing technology represented another leg of the rotation. AppLovin, which fell 13.4 percent on the week, is a prominent example of a name that had benefited from improving advertising budgets and product cycle tailwinds, but which can quickly re-rate when sentiment around consumer engagement, privacy changes, or competition shifts. Klaviyo’s 10.0 percent weekly decline, alongside LiveRamp’s 8.3 percent and Braze’s 8.1 percent, further illustrate how capital is rotating away from names with strong, but longer-duration, growth outlooks in favor of nearer-term earnings visibility. Sprinklr’s 5.2 percent weekly loss, together with milder declines at Zeta and The Trade Desk, rounds out the picture of a sector that is consolidating after a strong run.

Fintech displayed a similar dynamic, though starting from more modest valuation levels than many pure software names. Bill Holdings declined 8.5 percent on the week and 2.3 percent over the month, suggesting that some of the optimism around a clean macro and small-business backdrop has been tempered. Global Payments’ 6.0 percent weekly and 5.5 percent monthly declines reflect both sensitivity to consumer and merchant volumes and the broader shift out of more cyclical financial technology. Other names in the fintech bucket such as LPL Financial, Affirm, Arch Capital, and Synchrony posted smaller but still notable weekly declines. These moves underscore a market that is proceeding more cautiously toward consumer-oriented and rate-sensitive business models.

Consumer and digital commerce names also remained under pressure. Shopify’s 8.0 percent weekly and 1.8 percent monthly declines, GoDaddy’s 6.7 percent and 8.9 percent losses, Global-e’s 4.4 percent and Wix’s 4.3 percent weekly drawdowns, and General Mills’ 2.8 percent decline illustrate a wide-ranging de-risking across internet commerce and staples alike. There were bright spots: Nike gained 3.9 percent, and SEA added 2.9 percent, suggesting that where valuations are more reasonable, or catalysts more tangible, investors are still willing to selectively add exposure. However, in aggregate, the sector rotation narrative remains one of capital leaving high-multiple software, AdTech, and fintech and moving into semis and cyclicals.

In factor terms, this week’s action can be understood as a partial unwind of crowded growth and quality trades in favor of cyclicality and value within specific subsectors. Semiconductors and energy/industrials represented the “cyclical growth” poles, where secular demand (AI, data centers, energy transition, and infrastructure) intersects with cyclical operating leverage. Software and AdTech represented the “duration growth” pole, which underperformed as investors reassessed the appropriate discount rate and required near-term earnings growth for such names. The net effect is a rotational market that is still supportive of risk assets but is discriminating more sharply among business models, balance-sheet strengths, and the timing of cash-flow realization.

## Top Movers & Earnings Recap

Among the watchlist, Sable Offshore Corp. was the standout mover on the upside, advancing 37.5 percent over the week and 124.7 percent over the past month. Such a move, particularly over a relatively short time frame, implies a confluence of factors that may include improved perceptions of asset quality, contract awards, or shifts in expectations for offshore development activity. Given the absence of a near-term earnings catalyst in the next two weeks for watchlist names, this price action appears largely driven by flows and revised expectations for the company’s long-term cash generation profile rather than by fresh reported results. For portfolio construction, the key implication is that energy beta can reprice rapidly when investor interest returns, underscoring the importance of maintaining calibrated but meaningful exposure to the space.

Micron was another crucial positive outlier, with its 10.8 percent weekly gain and 34.7 percent monthly advance signaling continued enthusiasm around memory pricing and AI server demand. The stock’s performance reflects both cyclical tailwinds in DRAM and NAND pricing and structural tailwinds from AI training and inference workloads that require significantly more memory bandwidth and capacity. The magnitude of Micron’s one-month move suggests that a significant portion of the near-term earnings revision story has been priced in, but the underlying drivers—tight supply, disciplined capex, and diversified AI demand—remain intact. For active managers, Micron remains a core expression of AI infrastructure, but position sizing must account for the risk of consolidation after such a sharp run.

Sandisk, up 10.1 percent for the week and 41.6 percent over the month, shared many of the same thematic supports as Micron, particularly around storage and solid-state drive demand in data centers and edge devices. The stock’s even stronger monthly move relative to Micron’s indicates a catch-up dynamic as investors look for secondary and tertiary beneficiaries of the same AI and cloud secular trends. However, the sharper magnitude of Sandisk’s rally also implies greater sensitivity to any disappointment in pricing or volume trends, increasing the need for disciplined risk management. Names like Sandisk, which sit slightly down the market-cap spectrum, often respond more dramatically to changes in sentiment and positioning than their mega-cap peers.

Astera Labs and POET Technologies further exemplified investor enthusiasm for the broader AI hardware supply chain. Astera’s 7.3 percent weekly advance and 17.7 percent monthly gain reflect growing recognition of its role in interconnect and system-level optimization, which are critical for unlocking AI performance at scale. POET’s 5.1 percent weekly and 19.1 percent monthly gains underscore the interest in more specialized semiconductor architectures, particularly photonics and advanced packaging approaches that can alleviate bandwidth and power bottlenecks. Teradyne’s 4.3 percent weekly rise reinforces the idea that test and measurement equipment providers will benefit as semiconductor capital expenditure remains elevated.

On the downside, AppLovin’s 13.4 percent weekly decline, bringing its one-month performance to negative 6.6 percent, stood out as one of the sharpest corrections within the watchlist. This move likely reflects both sector-wide de-risking in AdTech and stock-specific concerns around competitive dynamics, changes in platform rules, or evolving expectations for user acquisition spending. While the longer-term narrative of data-driven, performance-focused mobile advertising remains intact, the near-term volatility in AppLovin illustrates that this is not a simple “beta-to-ad-spend” trade; rather, it is sensitive to product cycles, regulation, and platform relationships.

Palantir’s 11.1 percent weekly decline and 4.7 percent one-month loss highlight investor sensitivity to valuation and the pace of commercial AI monetization. The company has been a prominent beneficiary of the enthusiasm around AI platforms and government data analytics, and its stock had previously enjoyed a significant rerating. The current pullback likely reflects investors recalibrating their expectations for the timing and magnitude of revenue acceleration from new AI offerings, along with a general preference to de-risk high-multiple, long-duration stories during periods of macro uncertainty. Importantly, the fundamental thesis of Palantir as a differentiated data and AI platform remains, but the price paid for that thesis is undergoing a market-driven adjustment.

JFrog’s 11.0 percent decline and 4.8 percent one-month loss, together with MongoDB’s 8.3 percent weekly and 1.6 percent monthly declines, show that even well-regarded DevOps and database names are not immune to this valuation reset. Amplitude’s 8.4 percent weekly and 2.7 percent monthly drawdown reinforces this pattern in digital analytics, where investors may be questioning the durability of growth as customer optimization budgets tighten. LiveRamp’s 8.3 percent weekly and 6.1 percent monthly loss, along with Braze’s 8.1 percent weekly but still positive 10.8 percent monthly performance, completes the picture of a marketing- and data-analytics complex that is consolidating after a strong earlier phase.

Bill Holdings, with an 8.5 percent weekly decline and 2.3 percent one-month loss, serves as a cautionary example within fintech. Despite a compelling secular story around digitizing small-business payments and back-office workflows, the stock’s sensitivity to concerns about small-business health, competition, and margin sustainability remains high. Similarly, Global Payments’ 6.0 percent weekly and 5.5 percent monthly declines emphasize that scale and diversified revenue streams do not fully shield payments companies from sentiment-driven swings. For portfolio managers, these moves recommend a more discriminating stance within fintech, favoring those with clearer paths to sustainable free cash flow and defensible competitive moats.

Guidewire’s 8.7 percent weekly and 13.0 percent monthly decline illustrates the pressure on vertical software, while Tyler Technologies’ 5.5 percent weekly and 5.6 percent monthly declines and Manhattan Associates’ 5.1 percent weekly and 6.3 percent monthly drawdowns show that even steady, government- and logistics-focused software vendors are not entirely insulated. These companies typically trade at premium valuations due to strong retention, long implementation cycles, and limited competition. The recent pullback, therefore, likely reflects a re-rating from “best in class at any price” to “high quality at a reasonable price,” rather than any fundamental challenge in their end markets.

Across the entire watchlist, there are notably no earnings reports scheduled for the next two weeks. This absence of near-term company-specific catalysts heightens the influence of macro data, central bank communication, and cross-asset positioning on individual stock performance. Without earnings to reset expectations or provide new guidance, relative moves are more likely to be driven by changes in risk appetite, factor rotations, and technicals. For active managers, this environment places a premium on understanding the interplay between sector narratives, valuation, and liquidity, and on proactively positioning for potential inflection points when the next earnings season approaches.

## Macro & Rates Environment

The market action over the week suggests that investors remain highly attuned to the path of policy rates and inflation, even if there were no dramatic macro surprises in the last several sessions. While explicit index-level data are not provided here, the pattern of sector performance is consistent with an environment in which the probability of sustained restrictive policy remains non-trivial, and where the discount rate applied to long-duration cash flows remains elevated relative to the prior decade. In such a scenario, sectors like semiconductors and energy can outperform because they offer tangible earnings leverage to nominal growth and AI-related capex, while sectors like software, AdTech, and fintech—especially where valuations were most extended—can underperform as investors reassess the appropriate multiples.

Within this macro backdrop, the absence of concrete near-term earnings catalysts for our watchlist tickers means that macro data and policy signaling retain outsized influence on price formation. Every macro print that speaks to the trajectory of inflation, employment, or growth can shift the market’s expectations for the timing and magnitude of future policy moves. In turn, these shifting expectations are immediately expressed through relative performance: when the market leans toward a “higher for longer” policy path, higher-multiple, cash-flow-light growth assets tend to lag, while cash-generative, real-asset-linked exposures gain ground. This week’s rotation is consistent with such a regime.

It is also important to recognize that the AI investment cycle itself has become a macro variable. The scale of planned capex by cloud service providers, hyperscalers, and large enterprises into AI infrastructure—spanning GPUs, memory, storage, networking, and data centers—has created a quasi-secular growth pillar that is less sensitive to short-term fluctuations in consumer demand. Semiconductors like Micron, Sandisk, Taiwan Semiconductor, Astera Labs, and POET are direct beneficiaries of this trend, and their strong performance this week indicates that investors continue to view the AI capex wave as robust and durable. However, this same AI narrative has not yet provided the same level of support to many software names, where AI monetization is perceived as more nascent, competitive, and uncertain.

The interplay between macro and micro is also evident in energy. Names such as Sable Offshore Corp., Occidental, Devon, California Resources, Baker Hughes, and Comfort Systems rallied this week, reflecting an environment where investors see sufficient support in commodity prices and industrial demand to justify renewed exposure to energy and energy-adjacent services. The magnitude of Sable Offshore’s move, in particular, suggests that investors are willing to place higher probability on scenarios involving sustained or rising offshore activity. This is consistent with a macro narrative in which global demand for energy remains resilient and where geopolitical or supply-side dynamics keep a floor under prices.

Financial conditions and credit availability play an important role in the underperformance of fintech, AdTech, and certain consumer names. Companies like Bill Holdings, Global Payments, Affirm, and Synchrony are all sensitive to the health of consumers and small businesses, which in turn depend on the cost of credit and the robustness of the labor market. While there is no new quantitative data presented here on credit spreads or default rates, the price action suggests that investors are cautious about assuming further multiple expansion in these names without clearer signs that the macro environment is reaccelerating or that policy is on a firmly easing trajectory.

Given the lack of watchlist earnings in the upcoming two weeks, macro catalysts will remain front and center for relative performance. Any data releases or policy communications that shift perceptions of the future path of rates have the potential to reinforce or reverse the sector rotations observed this week. If incoming data were to meaningfully lower the perceived probability of sustained restrictive policy, one could envision a scenario where software, AdTech, and fintech outperform in a sharp relief rally, as the discount rate applied to their future cash flows falls. Conversely, if data and policy communications were to reinforce a “higher for longer” narrative, semiconductors, energy, and more value-oriented sectors would likely continue to enjoy a relative bid.

In this environment, risk management requires not only stock-specific analysis but also a clear framework for how portfolio exposures respond to changes in macro narratives. Portfolios that are heavily tilted toward one macro regime—whether implicitly or explicitly—may experience heightened volatility as the market tests different paths for growth and policy. A more balanced approach, employing a barbell between secular growers with demonstrated monetization and cyclicals with strong balance sheets and capital return, appears prudent. This week’s performance pattern validates such a framework.

## Watchlist Deep Dives

### Micron Technology (MU)

Micron’s 10.8 percent advance this week and 34.7 percent gain over the past month situate it as one of the key beneficiaries of both the cyclical memory upturn and the secular AI demand story. Investors are increasingly focused on Micron’s leverage to high-bandwidth memory and advanced DRAM modules that are essential for training and inference workloads in large AI clusters. The combination of tight supply discipline across the industry, steady demand from cloud service providers, and rising content per server is driving positive revisions to forward earnings expectations. This dynamic has translated into rapid multiple expansion and a sharp re-rating of the stock.

From a positioning standpoint, Micron’s recent performance raises the question of how much of the near- to medium-term good news is now priced in. While the underlying drivers of the thesis—AI-related server demand, tight supply, and disciplined capex—remain intact, the magnitude of the one-month move suggests that investors should anticipate potential consolidation or volatility as shorter-term traders take profits. Nonetheless, for long-term, fundamentally oriented portfolios, Micron remains an important core holding within the AI hardware ecosystem, given its scale, technology roadmap, and strategic importance to leading customers. The key is to calibrate position size to reflect both the upside case of sustained AI memory demand and the downside risk of cyclical corrections.

### Sandisk (SNDK)

Sandisk’s 10.1 percent weekly and 41.6 percent monthly gains underscore market enthusiasm for storage solutions that sit adjacent to the AI and cloud infrastructure build-out. The company’s exposure to solid-state drives, flash memory, and high-performance storage systems positions it well to benefit from both enterprise and consumer demand. As with Micron, the AI capex cycle is driving incremental storage requirements within data centers; each new AI server configuration typically requires larger and faster storage footprints, as well as optimized data pipelines.

The risk-reward profile for Sandisk, however, is somewhat different from that of Micron. The stronger one-month move suggests that investors may be pricing in a more aggressive improvement in pricing and margins, which could leave the stock more vulnerable to any disappointment in near-term metrics. Furthermore, competition in storage remains intense, with multiple large players pursuing similar customers and technology roadmaps. For active managers, Sandisk offers high beta to the AI storage theme but may require more active trading and tighter risk controls, given its sensitivity to sentiment and industry pricing cycles.

### Intel (INTC)

Intel’s 8.8 percent weekly gain, despite a 10.0 percent loss over the past month, reflects its status as both a turnaround story and a beneficiary of any renewed optimism about broader semiconductor demand. The company is in the midst of a complex transition from a predominantly integrated device manufacturer toward a more foundry-like model, with significant capital expenditure and execution risk. The strong weekly move likely represents a combination of short covering and renewed interest in legacy CPU and PC recovery narratives, rather than a clear resolution of the company’s strategic challenges.

For portfolio managers, Intel offers a differentiated exposure within the semiconductor space. It provides potential upside from any successful execution on its foundry ambitions and process technology roadmap, while also offering some cyclical leverage to PC, server, and edge compute demand. However, the stock’s risk profile remains elevated, given the scale of investment required and the intense competition from alternative architectures and foundry players. The recent rebound provides an opportunity to reassess position sizing and ensure that exposure aligns with one’s confidence in management’s ability to deliver on long-term targets.

### Taiwan Semiconductor (TSM)

Taiwan Semiconductor’s 5.5 percent weekly and 8.2 percent monthly gains highlight its continued centrality in the global semiconductor supply chain and AI hardware ecosystem. As the leading provider of advanced-node foundry capacity, TSM remains a key bottleneck for the production of cutting-edge GPUs, CPUs, and specialized AI accelerators. The market continues to view TSM as a high-quality, quasi-infrastructure asset within the semiconductor sector, with relatively predictable demand from a diversified base of high-profile customers.

The challenge for investors lies in balancing geopolitical risk, cyclicality, and valuation. TSM’s strategic importance and technological leadership support a premium multiple, but this is tempered by concerns about geopolitical tensions and supply-chain concentration. The current performance suggests that, for now, the market is focusing more on the near-term benefits of AI-driven demand and less on longer-term geopolitical tail risks. For diversified portfolios, TSM remains a cornerstone holding in any AI or semiconductor allocation, but position sizes should be set with an eye to potential exogenous shocks.

### Astera Labs (ALAB)

Astera Labs, up 7.3 percent this week and 17.7 percent over the past month, offers exposure to the critical but less visible layer of AI infrastructure: interconnects and system-level performance optimization. As AI clusters scale in size and complexity, bottlenecks increasingly emerge not only from compute and memory, but also from data movement and communication between components. Astera’s focus on connectivity solutions positions it to benefit as customers seek to maximize throughput and minimize latency in next-generation architectures.

The stock’s strong performance indicates that investors are increasingly attuned to the importance of these sub-segments within the broader AI value chain. However, as a relatively newer and higher-growth name, Astera is likely to remain more volatile than established large caps. Investors should expect a greater sensitivity to news flow, customer wins, and product roadmap updates. For AI-focused portfolios, Astera can serve as a higher-beta satellite position around core holdings like Micron and TSM, offering additional upside if its execution continues to meet market expectations.

### POET Technologies (POET)

POET Technologies’ 5.1 percent weekly and 19.1 percent monthly gains demonstrate the market’s appetite for more specialized semiconductor architectures that can address emerging challenges in power efficiency, bandwidth, and integration. The company’s focus on photonics and advanced packaging aligns with a broader industry trend toward heterogeneous integration, where multiple chiplets and functional blocks are combined to optimize performance and efficiency.

Given its size and developmental stage, POET should be approached as a higher-risk, higher-reward component of a semiconductor allocation. Its strong recent performance reflects optimism about its technology and potential design wins, but also amplifies the downside risk if timelines slip or competition intensifies. For long-term investors willing to tolerate volatility, POET can provide leveraged exposure to structural shifts in semiconductor design, but it should be sized conservatively relative to more established names.

### Sable Offshore Corp. (SOC)

Sable Offshore’s 37.5 percent weekly and 124.7 percent monthly moves are exceptional even by energy sector standards, highlighting a confluence of idiosyncratic and macro drivers. Offshore energy assets tend to be long-duration projects with high upfront capital costs and potentially significant long-term cash flow generation. The recent rally suggests that investors are reassessing the value of Sable’s asset base, possibly in light of improved expectations for offshore development, contract awards, or regulatory clarity.

From a risk perspective, such a rapid appreciation demands careful evaluation. It is possible that a meaningful portion of the move has been driven by short covering or momentum-driven flows, which can reverse quickly in the absence of sustained fundamental catalysts. However, the underlying theme—renewed interest in offshore energy as part of a diversified energy mix—remains supportive. For portfolios, Sable may be best treated as a tactical position rather than a core holding, with close attention paid to liquidity, news flow, and risk controls.

### Occidental Petroleum (OXY) and Devon Energy (DVN)

Occidental’s 6.3 percent and Devon’s 6.2 percent weekly gains situate them as more measured, large-cap expressions of the broader energy bid. Both companies provide exposure to oil and gas production, with substantial free cash flow generation and established capital return frameworks. The moves this week suggest investors are incrementally more comfortable underwriting continued strength in commodity prices and the sustainability of shareholder return programs.

For diversified portfolios, Occidental and Devon can serve as core holdings within an energy allocation, offering a balance between income, growth, and optionality on commodity prices. Their performance in weeks like this underscores the diversifying role energy can play relative to more growth-oriented technology exposures, particularly when concerns about inflation or supply constraints are elevated. Position sizes should reflect one’s view on the medium-term path of global demand and the regulatory environment for fossil fuels.

### California Resources (CRC)

California Resources’ 5.3 percent weekly gain, despite a 2.8 percent monthly decline, places it as a more tactical expression of the energy theme. The company’s operations are more geographically concentrated and often subject to idiosyncratic regulatory and environmental considerations. The recent rebound suggests that some of the earlier pessimism about its outlook has eased, but the stock remains more volatile than its larger-cap peers.

For active managers, California Resources can offer additional upside in an energy upcycle but also carries higher idiosyncratic risk. Given its more narrow asset base and regulatory exposure, it is best approached as a complement, rather than a substitute, for larger names like Occidental and Devon. Risk management should emphasize position sizing, diversification, and close monitoring of state-level policy developments.

### AppLovin (APP)

AppLovin’s 13.4 percent weekly decline and 6.6 percent monthly loss highlight the vulnerability of AdTech names to both sector-wide and company-specific headwinds. The company’s model, which hinges on performance-based advertising and the optimization of user acquisition across mobile platforms, is inherently sensitive to changes in privacy rules, platform policies, and competitive dynamics. The sharp weekly move suggests that investors may be reassessing the durability of its growth trajectory or the sustainability of its margins in an environment of evolving platform constraints.

From an investment perspective, AppLovin remains a leveraged play on the digital advertising cycle, with high upside potential when conditions are favorable, but also significant downside when sentiment turns. The recent drawdown may create opportunities for long-term investors who have conviction in the company’s technology and relationships, but it also underscores the need for a robust risk framework. Given the heightened volatility, positions in AppLovin should be sized conservatively and balanced against more stable holdings.

### Palantir Technologies (PLTR)

Palantir’s 11.1 percent weekly and 4.7 percent monthly declines illustrate the tension between a compelling long-term AI and data analytics narrative and the realities of valuation and monetization timing. The company has been one of the most visible public market plays on AI platforms, with strong positioning in both government and commercial domains. However, the stock’s prior re-rating had embedded high expectations for rapid and large-scale AI revenue generation, particularly from its newer platforms.

The recent pullback suggests that investors are now demanding clearer evidence of near-term AI monetization and a more tangible pathway to translating product launches into durable revenue and profit growth. For long-term investors, Palantir still offers unique exposure to mission-critical analytics and AI solutions, but the appropriate multiple for that exposure is being recalibrated by the market. In this context, the current consolidation may ultimately be healthy, creating a more balanced starting point for future appreciation driven by execution rather than by hype.

JFrog’s 11.0 percent weekly and 4.8 percent monthly declines, alongside UiPath’s 5.7 percent weekly and 6.9 percent monthly increases, highlight nuanced dynamics within DevOps and automation. JFrog, which focuses on software release management and artifact lifecycle, is leveraged to developer productivity and DevOps spending. Its recent weakness likely reflects concerns about IT budget prioritization and competition in the DevOps tooling space. UiPath, on the other hand, while down on the week, still maintains a positive one-month performance, reflecting ongoing interest in robotic process automation and AI-enabled efficiency tools.

For portfolios, both names represent differentiated ways to gain exposure to enterprise efficiency and automation. However, they also sit within budget categories that can be scrutinized as enterprises weigh discretionary IT spending against core infrastructure. The divergence in their one-month performance underscores the importance of stock selection within thematically similar groups, as the market increasingly discriminates based on execution, competitive positioning, and perceived pricing power.

Intuit’s 7.0 percent weekly and 2.8 percent monthly declines, Workday’s 6.8 percent weekly and 4.2 percent monthly losses, and Adobe’s 5.8 percent weekly but 2.0 percent monthly gain represent a meaningful, if measured, de-rating of large-cap application software. These companies have long been viewed as high-quality, resilient franchises with strong competitive moats and recurring revenue models. Their recent underperformance suggests that even the strongest software names are not immune to valuation pressures when the market rotates toward cyclicality and demands nearer-term AI monetization.

For long-term investors, the fundamental theses on Intuit, Workday, and Adobe remain intact. Intuit continues to benefit from its tax, small-business, and personal finance ecosystems; Workday from its leadership in cloud-based HCM and financials; and Adobe from its creative and digital experience franchises. The key question is not whether these businesses can grow, but rather at what price they should trade given the prevailing macro and rate environment. The current pullback may offer entry points for investors who had been waiting for more attractive valuations, but it also underscores the importance of patience and discipline in adding to positions.

Within cybersecurity, CrowdStrike’s 5.7 percent weekly and 13.5 percent monthly decline, Okta’s 5.6 percent weekly and 3.1 percent monthly loss, and Rapid7’s 7.3 percent weekly and 11.2 percent monthly decline highlight the sector’s recent challenges. The recent performance suggests that the market is rebalancing that consensus, demanding better alignment between growth, profitability, and valuation.

From an allocation perspective, cybersecurity remains a strategic priority for enterprises and governments, providing a durable demand backdrop. However, stock selection and entry points now matter more than ever. CrowdStrike, with its strong platform and customer expansion metrics, remains a core candidate for long-term exposure, but the recent drawdown argues for a more measured accumulation strategy. Okta and Rapid7, given their respective areas of identity and analytics, offer complementary exposures, but likely require operational and margin improvements to sustain premium multiples.

### Shopify (SHOP) and GoDaddy (GDDY)

Shopify’s 8.0 percent weekly and 1.8 percent monthly declines, and GoDaddy’s 6.7 percent weekly and 8.9 percent monthly losses, underscore the challenges facing digital commerce and internet platform names at this stage of the cycle. Both companies are levered to small and medium-sized business activity, online commerce formation, and digital presence. Their recent underperformance likely reflects concerns about the pace of post-pandemic normalization, competitive intensity, and, in GoDaddy’s case, the dynamics of domain and hosting markets.

Despite these near-term headwinds, the long-term secular trend toward online commerce and digital presence remains intact. Shopify, in particular, retains strong brand equity and a deep ecosystem, while GoDaddy continues to serve as a key gateway to online identity for small businesses. For investors, the current pullback may present an opportunity to selectively build positions, provided one is comfortable with the macro sensitivity of these names and the evolving competitive landscape.

Bill Holdings’ 8.5 percent weekly and 2.3 percent monthly declines, and Global Payments’ 6.0 percent weekly and 5.5 percent monthly losses, encapsulate the more cautious stance investors are taking toward fintech and payments. Bill’s model, which helps small businesses manage accounts payable and receivable workflows, is particularly sensitive to small-business formation and transaction volumes. Global Payments, though larger and more diversified, is still exposed to consumer and merchant activity.

These names remain fundamentally attractive over a multi-year horizon, as the digitization of payments and back-office workflows is far from complete. However, their near-term performance will likely track closely with macro indicators of consumer and small-business health. In this context, portfolios should maintain exposure to the theme but be prepared for volatility and potentially longer holding periods before the full thesis plays out.

## Upcoming Catalysts

Over the next two weeks, there are no scheduled earnings releases for the watchlist names, which places increased emphasis on macro data, policy communications, and sector-specific news flow as the primary catalysts for price action. The absence of earnings removes a critical mechanism by which companies can reset expectations, guide investors, and anchor valuation discussions. In such an environment, stock-specific idiosyncrasies are more likely to stem from analyst revisions, corporate announcements, M&A activity, or regulatory developments rather than from the traditional quarterly reporting cycle.

For semiconductors and AI infrastructure names like Micron, Sandisk, Taiwan Semiconductor, Astera Labs, and POET, the key catalysts will be any incremental data points on AI server demand, capacity expansion plans, and memory pricing. Industry conferences, customer commentary, and supply-chain checks can all influence expectations for the pace and durability of the AI capex cycle. Any indications of stronger-than-expected demand or persistent supply tightness could reinforce the recent rally, while signs of delayed deployments or cautious customer spending could trigger consolidation.

In energy, catalysts for names such as Sable Offshore, Occidental, Devon, California Resources, Baker Hughes, and Comfort Systems will include movements in commodity prices, updates on drilling and development activity, and any policy announcements affecting exploration, regulation, or environmental standards. Geopolitical developments and OPEC-related news can also act as powerful exogenous triggers. Given the magnitude of Sable Offshore’s recent moves, any company-specific announcements related to contracts, production targets, or capital allocation policies would be particularly impactful.

For software, cybersecurity, and AdTech names including Palantir, JFrog, Amplitude, MongoDB, Rapid7, CrowdStrike, Okta, AppLovin, Klaviyo, LiveRamp, and Braze, the near-term catalysts will center around investor conferences, product announcements, and any early read-throughs from peers or adjacent sectors. Analyst days and technical deep dives into AI product roadmaps can help clarify monetization timelines and competitive positioning. In the current environment, investors are likely to reward companies that provide concrete examples of AI-driven revenue uplift, improved unit economics, or accelerated customer adoption, while penalizing those that offer more generalized or longer-dated narratives.

Fintech and payments names such as Bill Holdings, Global Payments, LPL Financial, Affirm, and Synchrony will be sensitive to macro prints related to consumer spending, employment, and credit conditions. Changes in regulatory scrutiny, especially around fees, lending practices, and consumer protection, can also serve as catalysts. For these names, management commentary at conferences and in public appearances may play an outsized role in shaping near-term sentiment.

Consumer and digital commerce names like Shopify, GoDaddy, Global-e Online, Wix, Nike, and SEA will be influenced by high-frequency data on retail spending, e-commerce penetration, and promotions. Seasonal patterns, particularly around back-to-school and holiday planning, may begin to enter investor discussions, though the more immediate focus will remain on the trajectory of consumer confidence and discretionary spending. Any signs that consumer demand is more resilient than feared could support a rebound in these stocks, while evidence of further softness would reinforce the cautious stance currently embedded in their valuations.

Across the watchlist, cross-asset signals will also serve as important catalysts. Changes in interest-rate expectations, credit spreads, and volatility indices can all influence sector rotations and risk appetite. In the absence of earnings, these macro and cross-asset cues can dominate shorter-term price action, even when company fundamentals remain stable. As a result, aligning portfolio exposures with different macro scenarios and stress-testing for potential regime shifts remain critical tasks in the coming weeks.

## What To Watch Next Week

Heading into next week, the primary focus for buy-side investors should be on whether the observed sector rotations deepen, broaden, or reverse. The most important question is whether the move into semiconductors and energy, and out of software, AdTech, and fintech, represents a short-lived factor rotation or the beginning of a more durable re-rating across styles. Close attention should be paid to the persistence of flows into AI hardware names like Micron, Sandisk, Taiwan Semiconductor, Astera Labs, and POET, especially after their strong recent performance. If these stocks continue to outperform on relatively benign news, it would suggest that investor positioning remains underweight the AI hardware theme, leaving room for further upside.

Investors should also monitor whether software and cybersecurity names begin to stabilize after this week’s drawdown. For names such as Palantir, JFrog, MongoDB, Intuit, Workday, Adobe, CrowdStrike, Okta, and Rapid7, early signs of bottoming would likely manifest as narrower daily trading ranges, reduced volume on down days, and more balanced order books. Any positive commentary from management at conferences, particularly around AI monetization and customer demand, could catalyze a relief rally. Conversely, continued heavy selling and elevated volatility would indicate that the de-rating process is still underway.

In energy, the sustainability of Sable Offshore’s recent gains will be an important barometer of risk appetite in more speculative subsectors. A period of consolidation at higher levels, rather than an immediate mean reversion, would suggest that investors are gaining conviction in the underlying fundamentals driving the move. For Occidental, Devon, California Resources, Baker Hughes, and Comfort Systems, next week’s trading will help clarify whether this week’s gains represent the start of a broader re-rating of energy and industrial services, or a shorter-term reaction to macro or commodity-related news.

For AdTech and marketing technology, including AppLovin, Klaviyo, LiveRamp, Braze, Sprinklr, Zeta, and The Trade Desk, the key question is whether this week’s pullback has sufficiently reset expectations. Investors should watch for any incremental data on advertising budgets, campaign spending, and platform policy changes that could influence medium-term growth trajectories. If the sector can find a floor in the absence of negative news, it would suggest that the market is distinguishing between structurally attractive and more challenged business models. However, further downside in the group could indicate that investors are still re-evaluating the appropriate multiples for even the stronger franchises.

Fintech and payments names such as Bill Holdings, Global Payments, LPL Financial, Affirm, and Synchrony will likely remain sensitive to macro sentiment and any emerging data on consumer and small-business health. Next week, investors should pay attention to any shifts in the narrative around consumer credit quality, delinquency trends, or loan growth. Stabilization in these indicators could support a rebound in fintech, especially for names with strong balance sheets and diversified revenue streams. Yet, if macro commentary becomes more cautious, these stocks may continue to face headwinds.

Finally, at the portfolio level, next week presents an opportunity to reassess core and satellite positions in light of the rotations observed this week. For many investors, the emerging barbell of AI hardware and energy on one side, and high-quality but de-rated software and consumer names on the other, offers a robust framework for navigating the current macro environment. The goal should be to maintain sufficient exposure to structural growth themes, particularly AI and digital transformation, while ensuring that portfolios are not overly reliant on a single macro outcome. By closely monitoring sector performance, macro developments, and company-specific news, buy-side investors can position themselves to take advantage of dislocations and emerging trends in the weeks ahead.

market_summary:
US equities saw a sharp factor and sector rotation this week, with software and high-multiple growth names under pressure while semiconductors and select energy/industrial cyclicals outperformed. Broad index levels were choppy but resilient, as megacap tech leadership narrowed and dispersion picked up beneath the surface. Software infrastructure and application names sold off 5–10% in many cases, while semis and energy pockets posted solid mid‑single to low‑double‑digit gains.

Within the watchlist, software infrastructure, application software, cybersecurity and AdTech all traded heavy as investors faded crowded AI-adjacent and usage-based models, while semiconductors and energy/industrials attracted incremental capital. With no imminent watchlist earnings, the next two weeks will be driven by macro data, Fed communication, and positioning into mid‑year. Elevated single‑name volatility and cross‑sector dispersion argue for selective risk‑taking rather than broad beta exposure.

This sets up for more stock-picking and factor-driven moves rather than a uniform tech trade.
